archetype.name: Point Guard (late-career)
archetype.definition: At nearly 43, Rodgers wins by getting the ball out short and over the middle to whoever the coverage gives him, and no longer by stretching the field or creating outside structure.

report.headline: The quick game still works; third downs, shotgun sacks and the deep ball don't.
report.take:
Rodgers is a short-area distributor now, and the season splits make that plain. Throws of 0-9 air yards produce +0.327 EPA with a 73.2% completion rate and six touchdowns. Throws over the middle produce +0.602 EPA on 42 attempts. Everything that asks his arm or his legs to do more breaks down. Deep balls are 6 of 31 (19.4%, CPOE -15.6), throws to the left sit at a -10 CPOE, and his bad-throw rate (16.8%) ranks 34th of 36. None of this is new. His intended depth was 9.2 in 2016 and 6.0 last year, and his bad-throw rate was 16.5% in 2025. The overall line of -0.071 EPA per dropback (32nd) is what that profile costs when the offense keeps asking him to throw.

And the offense does keep asking. Pittsburgh's pass rate over expected is second in the league even though its run game ranks fourth in rush EPA. That is a strange choice for an offense whose passing ranks 26th. The formation split is the loudest number in the dossier. Under center he has averaged +0.326 EPA on 39 plays with no sacks and no interceptions. In shotgun he is at -0.195 on 159 plays, carrying all 14 sacks and all four picks. That isn't purely his skill: shotgun is where the obvious passing downs live. It still points to the same place. When defenses know he has to throw and hold it, the pocket collapses and he doesn't escape it, with three scrambles all year.

Third down is where it shows. He is converting 29.4% at an average of 7.3 yards to go, with -0.372 EPA and nine of his 14 sacks. His pressure-to-sack rate of 32.5% matches last year's 34.1%. He has always taken sacks rather than throw it away, and at this age he can't extend plays to make that trade pay.

The box score is kinder than the efficiency. Ten touchdowns rank fifth and his 5.4% TD rate ranks 14th, but red-zone EPA is -0.208 and three of the TDs came on 31 mostly failed deep shots. Expect the touchdown pace to drift toward his middling efficiency, not the other way around.

strengths.title: Short-area and middle-of-field accuracy
strengths.body: Inside 10 air yards he is efficient and accurate, and between the numbers he is the best version of himself (+0.602 EPA, 6.1 CPOE). Freiermuth's +0.265 EPA per target is the clearest beneficiary. This is processing and timing, the part of a quarterback that ages best, so it should hold.

strengths.title: Under-center efficiency
strengths.body: On 39 under-center dropbacks he has been strongly positive, with zero sacks and zero interceptions. Part of that is situation: these are early, run-friendly downs where the defense has to respect a top-four rushing attack. It still argues for a more balanced call sheet than McCarthy is running, and it is the game state where he remains a plus quarterback.

strengths.title: Recent form steadier
strengths.body: After a -21.4 EPA collapse at New England, he has posted positive passing EPA in three straight games and scored 22-plus PPR in each. Week 5 was a clean 22-of-31 with one sack. The Colts' 26th-ranked defense inflates that game, though.

concerns.title: Third-down and obvious-passing breakdown
concerns.body: On third down he converts under 30% and has taken nine sacks on 51 plays. Shotgun dropbacks carry every sack and interception he has. This is a real, age-related flaw rather than noise. His pressure-to-sack rate has sat in the low 30s for three seasons, and with almost no scrambling there is no release valve.

concerns.title: The deep ball is gone
concerns.body: He completes 19.4% of 20-plus-yard throws, with two interceptions and a -15.6 CPOE. He keeps attempting them, with a Week 4 aggressiveness rate of 27.5% and two picks that day. Three deep TDs have hidden how wasteful the bucket is. The career trend of shrinking depth says this won't come back.

concerns.title: Thinning receiver room
concerns.body: Pittman is on IR, and Roman Wilson, his second-most-efficient target at +0.254 EPA per target, is out, as is Skowronek. That leaves Metcalf and Bernard, who are both slightly negative per target, plus Freiermuth and the backs. With his margin this thin, losing the efficient short options hurts more than the raw target counts suggest.

trend.note: After two poor opening games (combined -29.2 passing EPA), he has been positive three weeks running, though Week 4 came with two interceptions and a 25.6% bad-throw rate, and Week 5 came against a bottom-tier defense.

nextGame.headline: Weak Bucs rush and a thin secondary, but his receivers are thin too
nextGame.body:
Tampa Bay is fifth in defensive EPA, built on a run defense that ranks fifth (-0.203 per rush). Offenses lean toward passing on it, and Pittsburgh already passes more than almost anyone, so volume should be there. The Bucs' pass rush is soft: 29th in hit rate and 28th in sack rate. That addresses his biggest weakness directly, giving him cleaner pockets on the downs where he has been getting buried. Their coverage has erased opposing WR1s (11.6 PPR under average, first in the league), which is a bad sign for Metcalf. It has been generous to WR2s and middling against tight ends, which nudges the ball toward Freiermuth and the short middle he already prefers.

Availability cuts both ways. Tampa Bay is without safety Antoine Winfield Jr. (97% of snaps) and corner Benjamin Morrison, which loosens the middle of the field. They are also without Baker Mayfield, against an offense already 27th in EPA, so Pittsburgh should play with a lead and shorter fields. On his side, Wilson and Skowronek are out and Pittman is on IR, while Rico Dowdle is expected back to support the run game. The early forecast shows 20 mph sustained wind with 30 mph gusts. It is five days out, but if it holds it pushes further toward the short game and away from the deep shots he already misses.

keyMatchups.title: His pocket vs. a quiet pass rush
keyMatchups.body: Tampa Bay rarely gets home, and Rodgers' sacks come from holding the ball in shotgun on known passing downs. If the Bucs can't win quickly, his third-down numbers should improve by default. It is the best structural edge he has had all season.

keyMatchups.title: Metcalf into a WR1 shutdown
keyMatchups.body: The Bucs have held top receivers far below their norms and allow -0.21 EPA per WR1 target. Metcalf already leads the team in targets without producing positive EPA. Forcing the ball there would be the worst version of this game.

keyMatchups.title: Middle of the field without Winfield
keyMatchups.body: With their starting safety out and tight ends drawing an above-league share of targets against them, the seams and short middle should be open for Freiermuth. That is exactly Rodgers' best zone.

nextGame.watch: Pittsburgh's third-down sack count: if the soft Tampa rush keeps him clean on obvious passing downs, this offense moves; if he's still going down, it's him, not the line.

restOfSeason.body:
The sustainable part is the short, middle-of-the-field distribution, a heavy pass volume driven by McCarthy's tendencies, and a functional run game. Those keep him around 230-250 yards a game with a steady floor. What should regress is the touchdown pace. A top-five TD count on bottom-third efficiency, propped up by deep scores at a 19% completion rate and a red zone that is negative by EPA, usually comes back toward the pack. Expect something like 1.5 TDs a game rather than two.

Interceptions could tick up. His bad-throw rate ranks near the bottom and his turnover-worthy count (4 INTs, 2 fumbles) matches his results, so his four picks aren't bad luck. The receiver room is short-handed until Wilson's late-October target date and Pittman's mid-November one. When they return, the efficient short options come back and the floor rises.
swingFactors: Whether McCarthy calls more under-center, run-first downs
Return of Roman Wilson and Michael Pittman Jr.
Third-down protection and his sack avoidance

bets.reason: Tampa Bay's offense is already 27th in EPA and 29th in passing, and it now loses Mayfield, while its own defense ranks fifth. Gusty early wind would add to that, though Pittsburgh's three straight overs and its 31st-ranked explosive-pass defense keep this from being a strong lean.
A Bucs offense facing Pittsburgh without its 98%-snap starting quarterback, plus a missing starting safety and corner, outweighs Tampa's strong run defense. Pittsburgh has covered three of five.
His 2.8 sacks a game come mostly from shotgun third downs. Tampa Bay ranks 28th in sack rate and 29th in hit rate, and he took one sack in Week 5 against a lesser rush.

confidence.note: Five games, but the core traits (short game, sack-taking, missing deep) match his last two seasons; receiver injuries and early wind add noise.
